content.summary: Guidance on use of high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays and rapid algorithms for early diagnosis of myocardial infarction (MI).
key_points: Baseline hs-cTn values vary with age, eGFR, time from chest pain onset, and sex, but absolute changes in hs-cTn remain diagnostically and prognostically valuable.
Until automated risk calculators that incorporate age, eGFR, time from chest pain onset, and sex are available, a uniform cut-off concentration should remain the standard for early MI diagnosis.
Because of higher sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy, hs-cTn assays allow shortening the interval to the second cTn assessment, reducing diagnostic delay and ED length of stay.
Recommended algorithms: 0 h/1 h algorithm is the best option; 0 h/2 h algorithm is the second-best option. The ESC 0 h/3 h algorithm may be an alternative where 0 h/1 h or 0 h/2 h are not available.
These algorithms were derived and validated in large multicenter diagnostic studies with central adjudication of final diagnosis for currently available hs-cTn assays.
Optimal thresholds for rule-out were selected to allow sensitivity and negative predictive value (NPV) of at least 99%.
Optimal thresholds for rule-in were selected to allow a positive predictive value (PPV) of at least 70%.
Three recent large diagnostic studies suggested the ESC 0 h/3 h algorithm balances efficacy and safety less well than more rapid protocols using lower rule-out concentrations.
High safety and high efficacy of applying the ESC 0 h/1 h algorithm have been confirmed in real-life implementation studies, including one randomized controlled trial.
Patients assigned to the rule-out pathway using ESC 0 h/1 h or 0 h/2 h algorithms have a very low rate of clinical events through 30 days.

recommendations.alternative_algorithm: ESC 0 h/2 h (second-best option); ESC 0 h/3 h can be considered when others are not available

content.evidence_notes: Algorithms were derived and validated in large derivation cohorts and then validated in large independent validation cohorts; real-life implementation studies (including an RCT) confirm safety and efficacy.
content.practical_implications: Use hs-cTn-based 0 h/1 h or 0 h/2 h algorithms where possible to shorten time to diagnosis and reduce ED stays; maintain uniform cut-offs until clinical tools adjust for demographic/clinical variables.
